assessmentSummary.identity: One Toe Yoga repetition is performed on one target foot. Begin with the target heel, first metatarsal head, fifth metatarsal head, and all relaxed toes supported. Lift only the great toe while toes two through five remain long and down, then return the great toe. Keep the great toe and first metatarsal head down while lifting toes two through five, then return all toes to the same start. That complete great-toe phase plus lesser-toe phase is one target-foot repetition. Record left and right separately. Standing hands-free, standing light wall-touch, and seated stable-bench support are explicit variants. Comfortable range, tempo, a brief untimed observation checkpoint, breathing, cycles per side, sets, rest, foot order, and delivery context are annotations. Simultaneous feet, manual assistance, resistance, sustained holds, single-leg or unstable support, toe spreading, toe curling, short-foot doming, whole-foot pressure shifts, compound actions, maximal assessment, and clinical treatment change the variant or definition.
currentCardFindings: Sources 45 and 524 execute the same great-toe then lesser-toe selective-extension sequence. Source 524's tripod, balance, and resilience language changes delivery context but not exercise identity, so it is a direct duplicate rather than a separate exercise.

The legacy cards do not define target-foot laterality, a complete two-phase repetition endpoint, side-specific counting, exact support variants, load and fatigue accounting, substitutions, persistence, or operational support. The canonical version supplies these without treating a participant label as an exercise property.

Direct activation research performed first-toe and lesser-toe extension seated and one foot at a time. Newer kinematic work also uses one target foot and documents unintended inter-toe coupling, so the card does not fabricate simultaneous bilateral mechanics or require forced perfect isolation.

Five YouTube candidates returned healthy oEmbed metadata. No candidate has been watched in full, assigned to an exact support variant, or approved for sequence, contacts, count, captions, accessibility, cue quality, safety, or card-version match.

Do not silently change support position, weight bearing, external hand support, target-foot sequence, simultaneous action, assistance, resistance, contraction mode, count, clinical scope, or task identity. Recompute logistics, duration, fatigue, substitutions, persistence, and coach and athlete rendering after every change.

calibrationEvidence.basis: Direct T2 MRI activation research, direct selective-toe-extension kinematics, a direct clinical sequence description used only for action wording, two intrinsic-foot training systematic reviews, a foot-strength exercise review, general supervised-exercise safeguards, the exact Source 45 and Source 524 contracts, five current YouTube oEmbed records, and comparison with short-foot, whole-foot pressure-shift, sustained hallux-press, toe-spread, toe-flexion, assessment, assisted, resisted, unstable, and compound neighbors
calibrationEvidence.uncertainty: Research does not validate one universal support position, range, tempo, dose, frequency, fatigue ceiling, recovery interval, warm-up effect, treatment, injury-prevention claim, balance or sport transfer, participant threshold, or Vortex difficulty score. Standing transfer is less directly studied than the seated target-foot tasks. No media candidate has been watched in full, and no relationship or score has qualified human approval.

claims: First-toe extension with toes two through five down and lesser-toe extension with the great toe down are distinguishable one-foot actions.
The exact combined two-phase cycle, support variants, side-specific count, and publication rules are Vortex specifications bounded by Sources 45 and 524.
Selective hallux extension and selective four-toe extension are active digit-motion tasks with explicit non-target ground-contact constraints.
The controlled taxonomy records a stationary braced foot-control task rather than locomotion, landing, toe flexion, or whole-foot pressure shifting.
Both selective toe-extension tasks increased activation across all measured plantar intrinsic foot muscles rather than isolating a single intrinsic muscle.
The card records toe extensors, plantar intrinsic and extrinsic stabilizers, MTP and interphalangeal joints, planes, target-foot laterality, contacts, and stabilization without promising isolation.
Non-target toe contact and unintended inter-toe motion are measurable features of selective hallux and four-toe extension.
The card permits comfortable active range and stops forced isolation, toe pinning, or compensatory foot and body motion.
The activation study could not infer individual task difficulty or muscle force from T2 change, while the actions require selective motor control.
The 42/8/42 standing hands-free projection and separate wall-touch and seated scores describe exercise complexity and physical difficulty only and remain queued for independent calibration.
Forty metronome-paced repetitions per foot produced measurable activation in a small healthy-athlete sample.

That laboratory exposure is not a universal workout dose; Vortex tracks actual cycles by side, active time, support, range, faults, symptoms, and overlapping foot exposure while recovery remains an estimate.
The studied tasks used one flat target foot, seated support, visible ground-contact constraints, and explicit non-target toe contact.
Vortex adds support-specific surface, hygiene, wall, bench, toe-visibility, symptom, communication, space, and exit constraints without turning demographics into exercise properties.
Intrinsic-foot training studies use varied interventions and outcomes rather than one universal dose.
Prepare and resilience ranges are quarantined examples and end before selective contact, toe length, arch, ankle, knee, body control, breathing, or symptoms degrade.
Toe yoga is described as great-toe extension with lesser toes grounded followed by the reverse action with the great toe grounded.
Vortex adds exact target-foot start, controlled returns, support variants, complete-cycle endpoint, side-specific count, faults, and stop rules without adopting treatment claims.
General exercise safeguards emphasize qualified instruction, safe equipment and environment, appropriate progression, and technique supervision.

No participant or age floor is inferred; symptoms, exact-task control, surface hygiene, toe visibility, support equipment, communication, cumulative exposure, and facility escalation policy govern selection.
Intrinsic-foot training may influence some foot and dynamic-balance outcomes across heterogeneous programs.
The exact cycle can serve preparation or standing-control context only when purpose and fatigue budgets fit; no universal balance, gait, sport, treatment, or prevention outcome is promised.
Selective tasks can show incomplete range and unintended non-target movement.
Athlete support emphasizes a small comfortable range, long toes, complete returns, quiet target-foot contacts, side-specific counting, and symptom checks instead of maximal or forced separation.
Ground contact and unintended motion of non-target toes can be observed during selective toe-extension tasks.
Coaches record support, side, target contacts, toe curl, phase order, complete returns, first fault, actual exposure, symptoms, and duration without diagnosing impairment.
Seated support reduces whole-body balance demand and focuses observation on toe control in the studied task.

The seated variant, visible phase cards, written sequence, smaller range, fewer cycles, more rest, captions, transcript, still images, or live instruction can improve access; assisted repetitions remain a separate variant.
First-toe extension, lesser-toe extension, toe-spread-out, short-foot, and toe-flexion exercises have different action contracts.

Support positions are exact variants; simultaneous, assisted, resisted, hold, unstable, single-leg, alternating-foot, split-stance, toe-spread, toe-flexion, short-foot, pressure-shift, assessment, and compound tasks retain explicit boundaries.
Five candidates returned current YouTube oEmbed title, channel, thumbnail, and iframe metadata on 2026-08-09.

oEmbed health does not prove playback, exact support variant, target-foot sequence, contacts, returns, count, captions, accessibility, cue quality, safety, reviewer identity, card-version match, or approval.
